item.title: 6,000 Flight Cancelled: US air travel resumption will ‘take time’
item.description: Flights in the United States were resuming on Saturday after being grounded for several hours due to a major communications outage, though authorities said returning to normal operations would take time. The nationwide stop on Friday sparked widespread chaos and left hundreds of thousands of passengers in limbo, with some pulled off planes moments before departure by airline staff who appeared in the dark about unfolding events. The incident marked only the second time such an alert had been issued in US airspace — which is among the busiest in the world — since the 9/11 attacks. The ground stop lasted around four hours and was lifted at 8:15 pm Eastern Time (0115 GMT Saturday). Federal Aviation Administration officials reopened the airspace on Friday night “after restoring full functionality” at air traffic control facilities, according to Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy. “It will take us time (to) resume normal operations… Our top priority is the safety of you and your family when you fly,” Duffy said. Administration officials blamed the incident on telecommunications issues with decades-old equipment, adding there was no evidence of foul play. “This is a legacy system problem,” Duffy said. “We have old, old switches, old routers. “We use 1980s little copper lines. It’s an old system that went down, and went down everywhere. It got overloaded.” Duffy had formally asked Congress on Thursday for $30.1 billion in funds to upgrade and modernize the air traffic control System. As the ground stop was lifted, he repeated his plea. “I’m going to say it a million times: the Congress has to give the resources to the president so he can finish this bill,” he said. 6,000 flights canceled There were almost 6,000 flights canceled, including some international routes, according to FlightAware, a tracking platform. Footage from airports around the country showed gates full, with planes waiting on taxiways. Passengers thronged concourses, desperate for information about an outage that had thrown their plans into chaos. “We’re trying to debate whether or not we need to reschedule or drive or what, but if the whole country is stopped, that means the highways are going to be jammed too,” said Joseph Anderson, 72, who was trying to fly from Las Vegas to Oakland, California. A nationwide ground stop is highly unusual. There was one such stop in January 2023 when a pilot notification system failed, but the only other national stop happened in the wake of the 9/11 attacks in September 2001, when no aircraft took to the skies for days. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin stressed there was no evidence of any hostile action on Friday. “We’ve seen zero evidence that this was a cyberattack or (AI) attack,” he told a news conference. He also ruled out any connection with the outage that affected Microsoft this week, knocking email systems offline for millions of users, public services and businesses worldwide. item.title: Delta 2027: Omo-Agege challenging political establishment he helped to build
item.description: By Egufe Yafugborhi For a politician who once occupied the number three position in Nigeria’s constitutional order, served two terms in the Senate and declared that he had completed his legislative assignment, Senator Ovie Omo-Agege’s decision to seek a return to the Red Chamber presents an intriguing twist in Delta State’s changing political history. More intriguing is his choice of Delta Central, the district he represented for eight years. He is now facing Senator Ede Dafinone, the incumbent he helped bring into the Senate in 2023, but who now belongs to the political establishment that has taken over the party Omo-Agege once controlled in Delta. It is a contest laden with political irony, bruised relationships and competing ambitions, raising questions about whether personal political capital can survive the collapse of an established political structure. Today, Omo-Agege is seeking a Senate return on the platform of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), while Dafinone remains the APC incumbent, backed by a party now accommodating much of Delta’s former PDP political establishment. From Ibori’s government to the Senate Omo-Agege’s political journey has taken him through government, opposition politics and national legislative influence. A lawyer, he began his major political career under former Governor James Ibori, serving as Executive Assistant, Commissioner for Special Duties and later Secretary to the Delta State Government between 2003 and 2007. After leaving government, he returned to private business and political mobilisation, eventually emerging as senator representing Delta Central in 2015. His re-election in 2019 elevated his stature further. He became Deputy President of the Ninth Senate, placing him among the most influential political officeholders from the Niger Delta. But in 2023, he abandoned the familiar senatorial contest to challenge for the governorship under the APC against Sheriff Oborevwori, the PDP candidate and successor to former Governor Ifeanyi Okowa. It was a bruising contest that divided political loyalties across Delta. Oborevwori eventually polled 360,234 votes against Omo-Agege’s 240,229, ending his immediate governorship ambition but not his political relevance. The Political Tsunami And The Lost Territory The defining rupture came in 2025. Before Oborevwori and Okowa moved into the APC, Omo-Agege openly challenged their proposed entry. At an APC stakeholders’ engagement in February, he declared that the two leaders had no moral ground to abandon the PDP, a party they had repeatedly described as insurmountable in Delta. He insisted they should remain in the PDP and rebuild the structure they had once celebrated. He argued that the APC had already established itself in Delta, winning two senatorial seats and other legislative positions in 2023, and did not need the wholesale arrival of politicians who had spent years presenting the PDP as unbeatable. item.title: 2027: Presidential choice exposes widening elite-grassroots divide in South-East
item.description: By Steve Oko, Regional Editor, South East The scene at the School of Health Aba, the commercial capital of Abia State last weekend offered a fascinating glimpse into what could become one of the defining political contradictions of the 2027 presidential election. It showed the widening gulf between the political calculations of South East power brokers and the apparent preferences of the ordinary people. It was a moment when political establishment encountered popular sentiment, and the response from the crowd was anything but pretence. The masses, in unmistakable terms, passed a strong message: they are not in for jokes! They know what is good for them. While a significant section of the South East political establishment, including governors, National Assembly members and other influential politicians, has either openly or tacitly aligned with President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s re-election ambition, the grassroots appear to be gravitating in a different direction, with the former Anambra State governor, and the Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, flag bearer, Mr Peter Obi, retaining a formidable following across the region. The drama unfolded when Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives, Rt. Hon. Benjamin Kalu, attended the 2026 Item Day organised by the Item people in Aba. Kalu hails from Bende town, a neighbouring community with Item. As a prominent supporter of President Tinubu, Kalu apparently saw the gathering as an opportunity to canvass support for the President ahead of 2027. He never wanted to miss the opportunity, and rightly so. But what followed was a political moment he might not have anticipated. He never dreamed of the dramatic turn of events as he grabbed the microphone to market Tinubu’s candidacy. Dressed in the traditional Igbo (isiagu) attire, with a red cap to match, Kalu who prides himself as ‘the number six’ man in the country, mounted the stage and urged the people to support Tinubu’s re-election, assuring them that the President would do more for Abia if given another mandate. ‘Tinubu’ to ‘Obi kererenke’ “Tinubu will do more for Abia. Vote for Tinubu in 2027. He is the best for Nigeria,” he told the gathering. But as the Deputy Speaker shouted “Tinubu”, apparently expecting an enthusiastic response from the crowd, what came back was a thunderous rendition of “Obi kererenke”, the popular solidarity chant associated with Peter Obi. The response was spontaneous, collective and blunt! Even with a microphone, Kalu’s voice appeared drowned by the surging chants of the crowd. Attempts to calm the gathering did little to change the mood. Neither his assurance of a proposed federal university for Item nor the intervention of a performing artiste, who quickly introduced another Tinubu campaign song, “On Your Mandate We Shall Stand”, could dislodge the crowd’s enthusiasm for Obi. item.title: Tinubu aide dismisses claims of convoy stoning
item.description: O’tega Ogra, Senior Special Assistant to President Bola Tinubu on Digital Engagement, Strategy and New Media, has disputed claims that the president’s convoy was attacked by youths following his attendance at Friday prayers at the Shagari Central Mosque in Area 1, Abuja. Tinubu had visited the mosque in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) for the Juma’at prayer on Friday. However, Dino Melaye, a chieftain of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), later shared a video showing some youths throwing stones at a convoy believed to belong to the president. In the video, which has circulated widely on social media, some of the youths were heard chanting, “Ba ma yi, ba ma so”, a Hausa expression meaning “we don’t want you; we don’t support you”. Reacting to the development, Ogra shared a separate video showing Tinubu leaving the mosque after the prayers. “Contrary to the narrative being pushed by the opposition, with videos of their alleged paid thugs at the National Mosque today, here is footage of Mr President leaving the mosque after Friday prayers this afternoon,” Ogra wrote. The footage showed Tinubu, dressed in a white outfit and black cap, waving to youths who cheered him and took photographs with their mobile phones as he made his way into his official vehicle. Ogra’s response challenged the account circulating on social media. However, the footage he shared did not independently establish whether the incident captured in Melaye’s video occurred at another location along the president’s route. The development comes amid growing concerns over political violence ahead of the 2027 general election. In a statement he personally signed on Friday, Tinubu warned politicians and their supporters against resorting to violence, saying security agencies had been authorised to deal decisively with thuggery and other anti-democratic activities. He condemned reported incidents of violence at political events across the country and urged political actors to focus their campaigns on issues affecting the welfare of Nigerians and national development. The president reiterated that violence had no place in political campaigns. The post Tinubu aide dismisses claims of convoy stoning appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: What has changed for Asaba since Azinge became Asagba?
item.description: By Egufe Yafugborhi When HRM Prof. Epiphany Chigbogu Azinge, SAN, ascended the throne of the Asagba of Asaba two years ago, he inherited an institution steeped in history, tradition and expectations. Today, the palace is becoming something more. A smart school has been built by the community and handed to the Delta State Government. Ambulances respond to emergencies. A drug rehabilitation centre has emerged. Security intelligence flows into the palace within minutes. Public spaces are being upgraded, a 1000-capacity Event Centre hosted guests to Nna Agu’s second coronation anniversary. Women are gaining a stronger voice in traditional affairs. Even long-standing practices such as community burials are being reviewed. For Azinge, the change is deliberate. He declared, “I’ve long migrated from being a traditional ruler, and now into traditional governance. I’m not only trying to think about the customs and traditions of our people. “I’m also thinking about the welfare, healthcare, education, among so many other things, to make sure my people, Asaba people, collectively, are very happy going forward.” It is a philosophy beginning to redefine what many residents expect from their traditional institution, the people building for themselves Perhaps nowhere is the new relationship between palace and people more visible than at the Asaba Community Smart Nursery And Primary School recently commissioned and donated by Asaba to the Delta State Government. Asagba Azinge sees it more than a building. “Today, Asaba is breaking new grounds. We try to shatter ceilings, if and when the opportunity presents itself. “I believe in the history of Delta state, and I dare say of Nigeria, this is the first time a community will come together, not just to build a smart school, but also have it donated to government” The project, he said, demonstrates that the traditional institution can mobilise the community while government provides the broader public-service framework. “It underscores our willingness, readiness at all times to partner our state government, complement their efforts, and support them in the growth and development of our state and our community in particular.” But the partnership comes with expectations. Standing at the school, Azinge turned to the government with a simple request: “If Asaba can donate a school to you, please donate a road to us so we can achieve this. Donate a road so people can access this place easily and then be able to school here.” For Delta State Commissioner for Primary Education, Chief Mrs Rose Ezewu, the message was equally clear. “This occasion is significant not merely because we are unveiling a new school facility, but because we are witnessing the power of community vision, responsible leadership and purposeful partnership in advancing the cause of education. “Sustainable progress requires collaboration with communities, traditional institutions, parents and other stakeholders.” A Palace That Listens If the school represent

item.title: Why 16 Nigerians died transiting through Addis Ababa
item.description: By Favour Ulebor, Abuja The Federal Government has advised Nigerians, particularly those with underlying health conditions, to exercise caution when travelling through Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, following the death of 16 Nigerians in the city this year. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs issued the advisory on Friday, revealing that Nigeria’s diplomatic mission in Addis Ababa recorded 16 deaths involving Nigerians transiting through the Ethiopian capital. The deaths were reportedly linked to health complications associated with the city’s high altitude. According to the ministry, Addis Ababa is located about 2,355 metres (7,726 feet) above sea level, where lower atmospheric pressure results in reduced oxygen levels. The ministry noted that while most healthy individuals can adapt to such conditions, travellers with pre-existing cardiovascular or respiratory illnesses may face increased health risks. “This year, Nigeria’s Diplomatic Mission in Addis Ababa has recorded 16 deaths involving Nigerians transiting through the city, reportedly linked to health complications associated with high altitude,” the statement said. The government therefore urged Nigerians whose medical conditions could be worsened by high-altitude environments to seek medical advice before travelling through Addis Ababa. “Travellers with underlying medical conditions are strongly advised to obtain appropriate medical guidance before undertaking such journeys,” the ministry stated However, the Federal Government stressed that the advisory was not intended to discourage Nigerians from travelling to or transiting through Addis Ababa. “Rather, it aims to ensure that persons who may be medically vulnerable to the physiological effects of high altitudes are adequately informed and encouraged to take necessary precautions,” the statement added. The ministry reaffirmed the government’s commitment to safeguarding the health, safety and wellbeing of Nigerians abroad through timely travel advisories and other consular support measures. item.title: Egemen Mustafa Şener on the three words he learned in a Black Sea village that still run his business
item.description: Çifteköprü is a small village in the Borçka district of Artvin, in Türkiye’s Eastern Black Sea region. It is the kind of place where the weather decides more of the week than any calendar does, where a neighbour’s word carries the same weight as a document, and where the ground gives back exactly what the work put in. It is also where Egemen Mustafa Şener learned, before he ever ran a construction site in Istanbul or a shipyard project in Montevideo, the three practices that still organise his business today. The three words, as the company itself frames them, are labor, promises, and land. From a Black Sea farm to an Istanbul construction site Şener was born in Çifteköprü in May 1968. His father worked the land, his mother came from a well-established Laz family, and the household ran on a set of unspoken rules that any rural community would recognise. Work was visible or it hadn’t happened. A spoken commitment was binding. The land did not reward shortcuts. When he moved to Istanbul after high school, into business school and then into agricultural trading in the late 1980s, those rules didn’t get left behind. By the early 1990s, when he had shifted into residential and commercial construction and was managing his first sites in the city, the same three practices were doing the actual work of running the business. The language of the construction industry was new, but the habits underneath it were the same ones he had grown up with. Egemen Mustafa Şener on labor, in a sector where everything has to be seen The first of the three is labor, and in construction it is not a metaphor. Every person on a site contributes something that is either visible in the finished work or hidden inside it. A good site manager is one who can see the work that is supposed to be hidden as clearly as the work on the surface. Visible labor is also what makes delivery possible. A project is a stack of promises about what will happen on which date, and every one of those promises rests on someone actually doing the work. When labor becomes abstract, delivery slips. In three decades of residential, commercial, industrial and infrastructure projects, this has not changed. The promise that does the work before the contract does The second word is promises. In most business settings, promises are secondary to contracts. In the one Egemen Mustafa Şener grew up in, they were the contract. A spoken commitment was held because the alternative, in a village the size of Çifteköprü, was impossible to live with. Transplanted into construction, that habit becomes a working style. A contract will specify the delivery date and the quality standard. But between any two reasonable parties, the real agreement is the one that was given before the paperwork caught up, and the business that honours that version tends to finish projects on terms that match what was actually said. item.title: Lumumba identifies what’s fueling xenophobia
item.description: •Says Africa cannot fight poverty by turning against fellow Africans Professor Patrick Loch Otieno (PLO) Lumumba has warned that Africa’s failure to create sufficient economic opportunities is fuelling xenophobia. He urged governments to address unemployment, poverty and weak industrial development rather than blame migrants for the continent’s challenges. Lumumba, a renowned Kenyan legal scholar and public speaker, said xenophobia often thrived in societies experiencing economic hardship, where unemployment, inequality and pressure on public services encouraged citizens to regard foreigners as competitors. He spoke as the keynote speaker at the Bridge Club’s grand end-of-year event in Lagos on Thursday. In his address, titled Africa Must Not Become Foreign to Itself: Xenophobia, Pan-Africanism and the Future of African Belonging, Lumumba argued that migrants were frequently made scapegoats for economic problems arising from poor governance and weak institutions. He said: “The foreign trader, worker or entrepreneur can be arrested. The failure to create productive employment over several decades cannot be arrested at a roadblock.” According to him, African governments must look beyond the presence of migrants and examine the structural weaknesses responsible for unemployment, poverty and economic competition. He said the inability of many African countries to industrialise and create productive jobs had forced millions of young people into informal economic activities, where competition for limited opportunities could generate resentment. Lumumba observed that Africa’s economic dependence on exporting raw materials while importing finished products had contributed to the loss of employment opportunities to other economies. “We export crude oil and import refined petroleum. We export cocoa and import chocolate. We export minerals and import the machines, batteries and technologies manufactured from them,” he said. He added that the continent was effectively creating employment opportunities elsewhere while its young population continued to struggle for limited opportunities at home. The legal scholar said the appropriate response to the exploitation of migrant workers was to enforce labour laws against employers rather than encourage hostility towards foreigners. According to him, employers who engage undocumented migrants and pay them below lawful wages create resentment among local workers while benefiting from the division. “The appropriate response is not violence against the migrant. It is enforcement of labour law against the employer,” he said. Lumumba also highlighted the contradiction in Africans celebrating the achievements of their compatriots abroad while treating migrants from other African countries with hostility. item.title: 2027: Violence threatens turnout as party supporters come under attacks
item.description: •60 to 70 per cent of voters afraid of voting – security analyst •INEC warns of N10m fine, jail term for inflammatory campaigns •Attacks on rallies, convoys heighten fears By Omeiza Ajayi ABUJA: Between 60 to 70 per cent of Nigerian voters are afraid that political violence will stop them from voting in 2027, a security expert, Mr Onyekachi Adekoya, has said, as voter apathy continues to rise. Adekoya spoke on Friday morning on The Morning Brief, a programme on Channels Television. He cited a calculation by Yiaga Africa. “If you look at Yiaga Africa’s calculation, 60 to 70% of voters are worried that political violence will not allow them come out on the day,” he said. He said that fear works against turnout. “Once the violence and the rhetoric of it goes up, people are less likely to come out to vote, and perhaps that is, some would argue, part of the strategy at play by some parties,” he said. There have been recent incidents, including attacks on party convoys and on an assembly in some states including Delta, Cross River, Lagos, Edo and Gombe states. In Delta State, a man was apprehended and not handed over to the police. He was then reportedly killed. Adekoya said violence was already rising and would get worse. “It is already ticking over 70 incidents captured so far,” he said. “This is not the peak of it because the campaign season has just started.” He said the stakes went beyond 2027, with politicians positioning for 2031 and 2039. “We expect that this political season will be a bit more violent and true to type,” he said. He said pressure on local politicians would raise tensions. “Politicians at the local level are under significant pressure to deliver on their areas and that would most likely raise tensions. What it will look like is that politicians use violence to destabilize the opponents in opponents’ area of strength so that they can lose votes.” Adekoya said his firm’s report classed 14 states as toss-up states, which would be “keenly contested”. He named the North Central, North East and North West, and parts of the South East, as areas of concern. “Nobody should die because somebody is trying to be president,” he said. On what security agencies could do, Adekoya said the shortfall lay in resources. “If at all there is a failure in security it is because of lack of capacity, poor logistics planning and the fact that we have a hydraheaded security problem which cannot be resolved,” he said. He said enforcement could not be left to the agencies alone. “There is a command structure where also politics get in the way of enforcement. It should not be a job only for the police, it should be a collective responsibility,” he said. The concerns followed a run of threats by office holders in several states in recent weeks, which has drawn condemnation from civil society groups, rights organisations and opposition politicians. item.title: Sacking of Atiku: What Justice Lifu based his judgement on
item.description: By Luminous Jannamike ABUJA – The leadership crisis rocking the African Democratic Congress (ADC) took a decisive turn when Justice Peter Lifu of the Federal High Court, Abuja, invalidated the emergence of Senator David Mark and other executives who assumed control of the party in July 2025. But the judgment of November 5, 2026, was not simply about competing claims to party leadership. It hinged on a fundamental legal question: could the party’s National Executive Committee (NEC) use its constitutional powers to replace an existing elected leadership structure without complying with the democratic procedures prescribed by law? In the Certified True Copy (CTC) of the judgment obtained by Saturday Vanguard, Justice Lifu said he identified critical weaknesses in the defendants’ case, including the disputed resignation letter on which they relied, the limits of NEC’s administrative powers and the absence of satisfactory evidence that the new executives emerged through a democratic election. The resignation letter One of the Mark-led camp’s principal arguments was that Nafiu Bala Gombe had voluntarily resigned as Deputy National Chairman on May 17, 2025, before the NEC meeting that produced the new leadership. The letter, tendered as Exhibit ADC 1, was intended to establish that Gombe had relinquished his position and consequently lacked the legal standing to challenge the subsequent leadership transition. Justice Lifu, however, was unconvinced Rather than accept the document simply because it was certified, the judge examined its signature against Gombe’s signatures on other documents executed before a Commissioner for Oaths. He explained that certification established the status of a document as a true copy but did not, in itself, establish the authenticity of a disputed signature. After comparing the documents, he said that he found material differences in their structure, style, formation and general manner of execution. “The signatures do not appear to be one and the same,” Justice Lifu observed. He consequently described the purported resignation letter as fictitious or fabricated and rejected it as reliable evidence that Gombe had voluntarily vacated his office. The finding removed a central pillar of the defendants’ argument that Gombe had ceased to be an officer of the party before the July 2025 transition. Importantly, this was a finding made in determining the civil dispute, not a criminal conviction for forgery. NEC’s powers could not override the law The second major issue concerned the extent of NEC’s authority under Article 19(14) of the ADC constitution. The defendants maintained that the provision empowered NEC to dissolve the existing National Working Committee (NWC), make administrative arrangements and install the new executives. item.title: South Africa releases Fani-Kayode’s speech after protest
item.description: South Africa’s presidency has released a separate video of Nigeria’s High Commissioner, Femi Fani-Kayode, delivering his address at a credentials presentation ceremony, hours after the diplomat protested its omission from the official livestream. Fani-Kayode had raised concerns after the live broadcast of Friday’s ceremony, at which he presented his letters of credence alongside 14 other ambassadors to South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, failed to capture his speech. The ceremony took place at the Sefako M. Makgatho Presidential Guest House in Tshwane, Gauteng, and was streamed on the South African presidency’s YouTube channel. The broadcast appeared to experience a technical interruption while French Ambassador to South Africa, Antoine Michon, was speaking. Fani-Kayode was scheduled to speak next, but the livestream cut to Ramaphosa’s address to the assembled diplomats. Reacting to the omission, Fani-Kayode suggested that his exclusion might have been deliberate, alleging that some elements in South Africa did not want to hear his views or see him. “Clearly some elements in South Africa do not want to hear what we have to say or see our faces, but we are here to stay as long as we are welcome and have the confidence of President Ramaphosa, which I am sure we do,” he said. He disclosed that he personally brought the matter to Ramaphosa’s attention during the photo session following the ceremony. According to the Nigerian envoy, the South African president took him to the relevant officials and acted promptly to address his complaint. Hours later, the presidency published a separate recording of Fani-Kayode’s speech on its YouTube channel. In the address, the Nigerian diplomat pledged to strengthen bilateral relations, particularly economic and diplomatic cooperation, between both countries. “Nothing can come between the two of us. And part of my job here is to reset that relationship, to come and build that bridge, and to ensure that whatever concerns we have mutually, we can work them out and move forward together,” he said. Recalling Nigeria’s support for South Africa during the anti-apartheid struggle, Fani-Kayode said the historical ties between both countries provided a strong foundation for closer cooperation. He described Nigeria as South Africa’s largest trading partner in Africa and stressed the importance of sustained collaboration between the two countries in advancing the continent’s interests. “Without South Africa and Nigeria working together, closely together, the destiny of our great continent may well be affected,” he said. Fani-Kayode also commended South Africa’s positions on international issues, including the conflict in Gaza, its participation in the BRICS bloc and its advocacy for the interests of the Global South. He praised Ramaphosa’s efforts towards securing Nigeria’s inclusion in the Group of 20 (G20), describing them as noteworthy and encouraging. item.title: Women and race to 2027
item.description: Going by the number of women that have emerged candidates in the last primary elections of all the political parties in Nigeria, next year’s general polls is bound to witness fewer number of women contesting elective positions. Weekend Trust reports that while more women indicated interests in contesting by obtaining forms to secure the tickets of their parties, most of them could not go beyond the preliminary stages, with many of them either withdrawing, not considered in the consensus arrangements, or defeated in the early stages. Checks by our correspondents revealed that a higher number of women had indicated interests in contesting for state assembly seats, but the number dwindled for those going for House of Representatives seats, again, dropping drastically for Senate and getting terribly low on governorship. When the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) released the names of the presidential candidates for 2027, only two out of the 18 candidates, which constitutes 11.1per cent of the total candidates, are women, despite making up 49.32 per cent of Nigeria’s population. The two women are Ada Elizabeth Okwori of the National Democratic Party (NDP) and Esther Iken Okereke of the National Rescue Movement (NRM). Also, there are four female vice presidential candidates who will be contesting. The figures indicate that fewer than one in every 10 candidates contesting the National Assembly elections is female, while women constitute just over one in every 10 presidential candidates. The Senate has the lowest female representation, with 123 women among 1,303 candidates, representing 9.4 per cent. The House of Representatives has 346 female candidates out of 3,560, representing 9.7 per cent. The figures reflect a pattern in Nigerian politics in which women participate extensively in elections but remain largely absent from the institutions where political decisions are made. item.title: World Diabetes Day: High cost pushes drugs, special diets out of reach
item.description: As the world marks the 2026 World Diabetes Day today, attention is once again drawn to the importance of early diagnosis, timely treatment and sustained care in preventing complications and saving lives. But for many Nigerians living with the condition, the challenge goes beyond early detection to affording medication, special diets and regular medical checks needed to manage the disease. Some patients who spoke to Weekend Trust said the rising cost of treatment had pushed them into financial hardship, forcing them to ration prescribed drugs, compromise their diets or go for days without medication. For Mrs Ngunengen Akpam, living with diabetes has become a daily struggle, not only against the disease but also against the rising cost of managing it. Tinubu booed at Abuja mosque after Friday prayers Women and race to 2027 The burden is compounded by her responsibility to also support her diabetic mother, Mama Lydia Acka, making the cost of medication, food and routine medical care a constant source of worry for the family. Akpam told one of our correspondents that the prices of essential diabetes medications had increased considerably over the years, making it increasingly difficult to maintain the treatment prescribed by her doctors. She recalled that Metformin, one of the drugs she takes, which sold for N700 for a pack of three cards in 2015, now costs about N2,500. Similarly, Dormin, which previously sold for N700, now costs N3,500 for a pack of 10 cards, she said. “The cost of drugs has increased tremendously. I take my medication twice daily, so it is not easy. In a month, we spend so much, especially when you have another diabetic person to cater for,” she said. Medication, however, is only part of the financial burden. Akpam explained that managing diabetes also requires adherence to a carefully regulated diet, including millet, beans and vegetables, which have also become expensive. Although the price of millet had dropped from more than N1,200 to N600 per mudu during the harvest season, she said her financial circumstances still made it difficult to consistently afford the recommended food items. The experience is similar for Mrs Elahi Onu, who has lived with diabetes for 11 years and whose treatment has become a major financial responsibility for her children. Onu said her children spend at least N25,000 monthly on medication alone, while more than N60,000 goes into providing the special diet recommended for managing her condition. She listed unripe plantain, beans, vegetables, basmati rice and grains such as millet among the food items she had been advised to eat. “These special types of food are costly and drain the pockets of my children. “Sometimes there is a delay in supplies of these items to me. I will be forced to go hungry for the period or fall back to any available food,” she said. item.title: Amidst campaigns, Borno, Niger children remain in captivity
item.description: As the campaign season hots up, families of the abducted children in Borno and Niger states are still looking up to the authorities for intervention. Weekend Trust reports that while the pupils kidnapped in Borno have spent 213 days in captivity, students abducted in Niger have also remained in the hands of their captors for more than two weeks. Today makes it 213 days of agony and sleepless nights for the families of the abducted children in Mussa and Lassa communities of Askira-Uba Local Government Area in Borno State. The78 children, including toddlers less than two years old, who were abducted following two separate operations by bandits and insurgents, are still in captivity, even as politicians intensify campaigns for political power. The nightmare began on May 15, 2026 when at least 42 pupils and students were taken from their classrooms in Mussa Primary and Secondary School. Weeks later, on June 29, another set of 36 students were abducted in Government Day Secondary School, Lassa, further escalating security concerns in the area. Women and race to 2027 How IDPs built Abuja’s largest beans market Since then, the whereabouts of the children have remained unknown, plunging the families into a state of painful trauma. The Mussa school children were abducted on the same day as the 44 pupils and teachers from a school in the Oriire Local Government Area of Oyo State. But unlike the Mussa schoolchildren that have remained in captivity, the Oyo children were rescued on July 10, 2026 after 56 days in captivity after President Bola Ahmed Tinubu gave marching orders to heads of security operatives to rescue them. Weekend Trust reports that parents of the abducted pupils in Borno have on various occasions expressed frustration over what they described as “silence” from both the federal and state governments. The families are alleging that the authorities have entirely abandoned them; expressing fear that their children may have been forgotten by the same people they voted to power to protect them. The chairman of the parents of the abducted children, Mr Ishaku Suya, told our correspondent that the communities had remained in despair since the abduction of the schoolchildren. “Officially, I have not heard anything from the federal or state governments. Nobody is saying anything. And nobody has reached out to us from the side of the abductors,” he said. According to him, the mothers of the abducted children are always crying and thinking about their condition. “As men, we cannot cry, but we can’t eat food whenever we remember that our toddlers, some of them less than 2 years old, are still in the hands of their abductors. We all feel abandoned,” he said. item.description: …Group alleges 22-year concealment of registered constitution ..Dispute over rotational principle, five-year tenure of Ikenge . ..Cabinet scribe distances self, blames PG’s kinsmen By Steve Oko A leadership crisis has erupted in Eziowa, Aguobu Owa Autonomous Community, Ezeagu Central Local Government Area of Enugu State, over the interpretation of the community’s constitution and the emergence of a new President-General of its Town Union. The crisis centres on allegations by a group, Concerned People of Eziowa, that a part of the community’s constitution, registered on February 8, 2004, was kept away from the people for about 22 years, resulting in disagreements over leadership succession and the tenure of traditional and town union office holders. The group, in a statement signed by Ozo Dr Ejike Orji on its behalf, alleged that a Certified True Copy (CTC) of the constitution initially made available to the community did not contain Page 23, which it said contains provisions governing the tenure and selection of members of the Igwe’s Cabinet and the office of Ikenge. It said a subsequent search at the Enugu State Ministry of Local Government and Chieftaincy Affairs enabled it to obtain another certified copy containing the disputed page. According to the group, the provisions of Page 23 stipulate a five-year review of the tenure of members of the Igwe’s Cabinet and provide for rotational occupation of the office of Ikenge among the community’s three villages, excluding the village that produces the reigning traditional ruler. It alleged that the office of Ikenge had remained with one individual beyond the stipulated period, arguing that the position was due for rotation between Ezema and Umudim villages. The group also cited Article Seven (1) of Page 12 of the constitution, which it said provides for a four-year tenure for the President-General and other Town Union executive members. It maintained that, following the expiration of the tenure of the previous executive in 2024, the process of electing a successor commenced in line with the constitutional provisions. According to the statement, Ezema Village, which it claimed was next in line to produce the President-General, constituted an electoral committee that conducted elections into the positions allocated to the village and announced the winners. However, the group alleged that disagreement arose after some stakeholders accepted the outcome of the village electoral committee in respect of other positions but rejected its choice of candidate for the office of President-General. It claimed that some stakeholders were insisting on a different candidate and had approached the state ministry over recognition of their preferred choice. The group, however, maintained that its preferred candidate emerged through the process prescribed by the community’s constitution. item.description: By Dickson Omobola Experts in the aviation sector have called for stricter oversight of private and charter aircraft operators in the country and urged relevant agencies to strengthen flight surveillance, improve information-sharing and impose stiffer sanctions on operators found violating aviation regulations. The experts raised concerns over regulatory enforcement following two recent serious incidents involving private aircraft: a private jet, registration number N989BC, operated by VMO Aero Ltd, which landed on a road in the Ogwashi-Uku area of Delta State, and a Challenger 604 aircraft, registration number T7-SEI, operated by Triton Aviation, whose crew reported that a door had opened in flight They particularly questioned the handling of the Asaba incident and raised concerns about the absence of a final investigation report and the enforcement actions taken against the pilot and the company responsible for managing the aircraft. One of the experts also queried the regulatory oversight of foreign-registered private jets operating in Nigeria, alleging that some operators might be exploiting their connections to influential individuals to evade regulatory requirements. Yes, there was a preliminary report, but I think we want to know what happened to that pilot. Are they not supposed to prosecute the pilot? What about the organisation that managed that aircraft? “I don’t think we should panic (both incidents). There is no red flag as far as I am concerned. item.title: US Flight Ground Stop: What we know about disruption
item.description: The United States has lifted a nationwide flight ground stop that lasted more than four hours, marking the longest shutdown of departing flights since the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) attributed Friday’s disruption to what it described as “extraordinary circumstances” arising from a communications failure affecting air traffic control centres across the country. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication that the incident resulted from an attack, assuring that passengers and aviation personnel were safe throughout the disruption. Here are the major details of the incident. How many flights were affected? The ground stop resulted in more than 8,500 flight delays and nearly 8,000 cancellations on Friday, according to flight-tracking service FlightAware. The FAA initially announced the restriction at 3:54 p.m. Eastern Standard Time (20:54 GMT), directing that all departing flights within the United States remain grounded until further notice. More than 3,500 aircraft were airborne when the order was issued. While some were diverted to alternative airports, others continued to their intended destinations. Several hours later, the FAA began allowing limited departures, including flights from San Francisco International Airport. The agency officially reopened US airspace at 8:15 p.m. Eastern Time (01:15 GMT on Saturday). What happened to international flights? The disruption also affected international aviation, with flights bound for the United States from countries within the European Organisation for the Safety of Air Navigation, known as Eurocontrol, suspended at the FAA’s request. Eurocontrol confirmed on its website that the suspension was due to technical problems affecting US aviation operations. The organisation has 42 member states, including European Union countries, the United Kingdom, Ukraine, Turkey, Israel and Morocco. Sydney Airport, Australia’s largest international airport, also grounded all US-bound flights pending further notice. Air Canada equally cancelled flights between the United States and Canada. When will normal flight operations resume? Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy warned that the disruption would have consequences for airline operations over several days, even after the ground stop was lifted. “It’s going to take us some time to unwind what’s happened this afternoon,” he said at a news conference on Friday night. Duffy disclosed that tens of thousands of passengers were stranded at airports across the country, with many uncertain about where they would spend the night. Major airlines announced different recovery plans following the reopening of US airspace. Delta Air Lines and United Airlines said they were resuming operations, while American Airlines said it was working to operate as many remaining flights as possible that evening. item.title: Ageing US air traffic equipment triggers repeated flight disruptions
item.description: The nationwide grounding of departing flights across the United States on Friday was the second such shutdown since the September 11, 2001, attacks, highlighting recurring problems with ageing air traffic control equipment and communications infrastructure. The latest disruption, which affected air traffic control centres across the country, is part of a series of technical failures that have repeatedly disrupted flight operations in the US over the past three years. Although Congress approved $12.5 billion last year to upgrade the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) ageing air traffic control systems and recruit more controllers, the Trump administration is seeking an additional $30 billion to complete the modernisation programme. Recent incidents have exposed vulnerabilities in the country’s aviation infrastructure, with communications outages, data-link failures and automation problems causing widespread delays and cancellations. Major disruptions in recent years November 13, 2026: Nationwide ground stop The FAA grounded all departing flights across the US after air traffic control centres experienced a communications outage. According to flight-tracking service FlightAware, airlines cancelled more than 1,000 flights and delayed nearly 10,000 others. September 21, 2026: East Coast disruption The FAA suspended flights to airports in New York, Philadelphia, Boston and Washington for eight hours after the primary and backup data links at the Philadelphia regional air traffic control facility failed. The incident resulted in about 9,500 flight delays and cancellations across the country. The disruption coincided with the arrival of 130 world leaders in New York for the annual high-level meeting of the United Nations General Assembly. Dallas and Denver disruptions A data service outage at the FAA’s Dallas Terminal Radar Approach Control (TRACON), which manages aircraft movements between airports and higher-altitude airspace, forced the agency to impose ground stops at two airports in the Dallas area. More than 1,800 flights were delayed, while hundreds were cancelled. The FAA subsequently said contractor L3Harris had failed to ensure that backup systems were in place. However, L3Harris told NBC 5 in Dallas that the outages were preventable and resulted from inadequate US government investment in replacing outdated analogue telecommunications circuits that had reached the end of their operational life. A day before the Dallas incident, a separate automation failure in Denver forced the FAA to slow flights into Denver International Airport, resulting in average delays of between 30 and 45 minutes. April-May 2025: Newark and Philadelphia Several telecommunications outages over a number of weeks at the FAA’s Philadelphia TRACON repeatedly disrupted flight operations at Newark Liberty International Airport in New Jersey. item.title: US resumes flights after nationwide air traffic failure
item.description: The United States has reopened its airspace after a nationwide ground stop triggered by a communications failure at air traffic control centres disrupted thousands of flights and left tens of thousands of passengers stranded at airports across the country. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lifted the restriction on Friday, with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announcing that US airspace reopened at 8:15 p.m. Eastern Time (0115 GMT on Saturday). However, Duffy warned that flight operations would resume gradually, adding that airlines would need time to restore normal schedules. “It’s going to be slow,” he told reporters at the White House. According to flight-tracking platform FlightRadar24, more than 6,600 flights were cancelled and 8,600 delayed, while another 1,500 flights had already been cancelled for Sunday. Aviation analysts warned that the four-hour nationwide grounding could disrupt airline operations for several days. Duffy said tens of thousands of passengers were stranded at airports nationwide following the disruption. He disclosed that he and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin had met with President Donald Trump at the Oval Office to discuss the incident. What caused the disruption Duffy said the problem began at 3:36 p.m. when air traffic control centres experienced instability in their radar and communications systems. According to him, switches and routers became overloaded with data, resulting in inconsistencies in information transmitted through the network and prompting authorities to shut down the affected system. “Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data and they started to give us inconsistencies in the data from those routers and because of that we shut the system down,” he said. He maintained that authorities never completely lost radar or communications capabilities and were able to land thousands of aircraft safely. Duffy said the immediate technical problem had been resolved and that flying was safe, but stressed the need for a comprehensive upgrade of the country’s ageing air traffic control infrastructure. FG seeks $50bn for aviation overhaul The Transportation Secretary blamed inadequate congressional funding for delays in modernising the country’s air traffic control system, calling for $50 billion to overhaul the infrastructure. Earlier on Friday, before the disruption, the White House and the Department of Transportation had urged Congress to approve $30.1 billion for upgrades to the nation’s ageing airports and air traffic control infrastructure. “What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system,” Duffy said. “Give us the money to fix it.” Meanwhile, Mullin said there was no evidence so far that the incident resulted from a cyberattack or a rogue artificial intelligence system, although investigators had not ruled out either possibility. “It appears this was mechanically driven, however, we’re still looking,” he said. item.title: How IDPs built Abuja’s largest beans market
item.description: Ibrahim Philemon was compelled to abandon everything he had built in his youth and flee his native Gwoza for Karu in Nasarawa State because of Boko Haram’s relentless attacks on his community. Philemon is among thousands of other farmers who fled their towns because of intensified security risks posed by Boko Haram militants. But these farmers, despite facing adversity, remained undeterred. As internally displaced persons (IDPs), they were determined to rebuild their lives after the devastation caused by Boko Haram. Today, Philemon produces over 100 bags of beans and over 50 bags of maize annually since coming to Karu in 2013 as an internally displaced person. Amidst campaigns, Borno, Niger children remain in captivity Tinubu booed at Abuja mosque after Friday prayers When Boko Haram captured Gwoza town, which had an estimated population of around 388,600 in August 2014, thousands fled immediately to many states in the country and the neighbouring towns in Cameroon. Gwoza, which is located on the fringes of Sanbisa forest, is about 135 kilometres southeast of Maiduguri, the capital of Borno State. It is marked by a hilly terrain. As farmers, the displaced persons established approximately 13 camps in Karu Local Government Area of Nasarawa State, where they commenced agricultural activities. With an estimated population of over 20,000, according to the International Organisation for Migration in Nasarawa, the IDPs spread across farming communities in Karu and Keffi, seeking farmlands and clearing bushes and forests that were hitherto uncultivated to plant beans and maize. Some of them harvested over 200 bags of beans (cowpea) and maize. Within three years of their arrival, these displaced farmers rose from the ashes to establish one of the most vibrant grain markets on the outskirts of Abuja, the country’s capital, which today attracts buyers across the country. Setting up a beans market As they continued to record good harvests, selling their produce in good value immediately became a huge challenge that devastated many of them who were trying to find life after the colossal losses inflicted on them back home in Gwoza. That challenge gave birth to the establishment of what is today known as the foremost beans market in 2016, located in Auta Balefi, along the Abuja-Keffi expressway, about 25 kilometres from the Aso Rock Villa, before the National Agricultural Showground. They told our reporter, who spent a day with them, that farming and trading provided opportunities for them to rebuild their lives after displacement. David Yakubu, the secretary of the beans market, told Weekend Trust how the idea came about. He said the market was established after they encountered difficulties selling their agricultural produce at profitable prices in Ibadan, Oyo State. item.title: Emperor, 8,000 soldiers and lesson for Nigeria
item.description: I came looking for ancient soldiers and left thinking about Nigeria’s tourism potential. One thing I was particularly looking forward to during my visit to China was seeing the famous Terracotta Warriors in Xi’an. I had read about them, seen pictures, and of course, watched films inspired by the mysteries of ancient China. But nothing quite prepared me for the experience of standing in front of thousands of life-sized soldiers who have been buried underground for more than 2,000 years. And what an experience it was! If you have watched Hollywood’s The Mummy: Tomb of the Dragon Emperor, you may remember the mysterious army of clay soldiers that comes alive. Well, I finally got to see the real thing. Thankfully, none of them came alive while I was there. But standing in those enormous exhibition halls, surrounded by thousands of soldiers, horses and chariots arranged in military formation, I couldn’t help wondering what must have gone through the minds of the people who created this extraordinary army. The story takes us back to 221 BC when Qin Shi Huang became the first emperor to unify China. Like many powerful rulers of his time, he was obsessed with immortality and the idea of continuing his reign beyond death. His solution was to build an entire underground army to protect him in the afterlife. Think about that. While some people prepared for retirement, this emperor was preparing for eternity, complete with his own military formation. The scale of the project is difficult to comprehend. Thousands of life-sized clay soldiers, horses and chariots were painstakingly created. Above the excavation pit in Xi’an, I stood where visitors have looked down on the Terracotta Army for decades: thousands of figures, each made by hand, and still not fully unearthed. What makes the discovery even more fascinating is that the soldiers are not identical. They have different facial features, hairstyles, uniforms and expressions. They look like real individuals, each with a distinct identity and military rank. Then comes another remarkable twist. For over 2,000 years, this enormous army remained hidden beneath the earth until 1974 when some local farmers digging a well stumbled upon fragments of what would become one of the greatest archaeological discoveries in modern history. Imagine going out to dig a well and discovering an entire army. I wonder what the conversation was like that evening when they returned home. Today, the site is recognised globally as one of the greatest archaeological treasures in the world, and is popularly described as the Eighth Wonder of the World. The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO) designated the Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor a World Heritage Site in 1987. But beyond the fascinating history, what struck me most was what China has done with this discovery. This is where the story becomes particularly interesting for Nigeria. item.title: Who Gets To Compete?
item.description: Opposition talks are continuing. Campaigns are gathering pace. But access, legal certainty and confidence in the vote are becoming defining questions of the election. In Yelwata, Peter Obi stood before a community carrying the wounds of mass violence. In Akure, the APC called its organisation to work for President Bola Tinubu’s re-election. In London, INEC’s chairman faced questions about whether Nigerians could trust the coming vote. These were different settings for the same election. Together, they reveal a contest in which persuading voters is only part of the task. Candidates must sustain their organisations, establish their right to participate and reach citizens safely. The electoral commission must demonstrate that those citizens’ choices will be recorded faithfully. The week’s developments sharpen a fundamental question: how open, credible and competitive will the road to 2027 remain? Lagos Raises the Stakes Thursday’s reported attack on an NDC town hall gathering in Oregun, Lagos, deserves particular attention. According to reporting from the scene, armed men disrupted the gathering, participants were injured and a suspect was arrested. The NDC alleged political responsibility; the Lagos APC denied sponsoring the incident. The report established no independent evidence linking the attackers to a political party. Investigation must establish who acted, who organised them and whether anyone provided support. The democratic principle requires no such delay: citizens must be able to attend lawful political meetings without fearing assault. Violence can influence an election before a ballot is cast. It can discourage attendance, make venues reluctant to host meetings, increase campaign costs and persuade volunteers to stay home. Its effects therefore extend beyond the immediate victims. When intimidation restricts participation, it changes the conditions under which candidates compete. Political leaders should condemn attacks consistently, including when the victims support their opponents. Security agencies must provide protection on the same basis. Makinde Keeps the Alliance Door Open Seyi Makinde’s latest comments give fresh substance to the opposition’s continuing conversation about cooperation. In an interview reported today, the Oyo governor confirmed active discussions involving Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi. He said decisions should draw on evidence, manifestos, previous performance and public sentiment. He did not announce an agreement or endorse a preferred candidate. That distinction separates a development worth watching from a coalition already formed. The negotiations face a familiar practical difficulty: cooperation requires choices that impose costs on participants. Someone may need to surrender an ambition, accept another candidate’s leadership or persuade supporters to work with former rivals. An agreement also needs to travel beyond the negotiating room. item.title: Tinubu Hails Bakassi Seaport, Says Project Will Create Jobs, Boost Trade
item.description: President Bola Tinubu has described the groundbreaking of the Bakassi Deep Seaport in Cross River State as a major milestone in Nigeria’s economic diversification, saying the project will open new commercial corridors, stimulate industrialisation and create jobs. Represented by Vice President Kashim Shettima at the ceremony in Bakassi on Friday, November 13, 2026, Tinubu commended Governor Bassey Otu and the people of Cross River for sustaining the project’s vision and moving it towards actualisation. The President recalled that the project was conceived in 2014, with an Environmental and Social Impact Assessment developed in March 2015, before receiving fresh impetus under Otu. Designed with a 20-metre draft, the port is expected to accommodate large vessels that currently bypass Nigerian ports. It is also linked to a 260-kilometre superhighway intended to facilitate the movement of cargo to markets across the country. Tinubu credited Otu’s determination with helping to overcome institutional and financial challenges, including efforts to secure a $3.5 billion financing arrangement with Afreximbank and formalise the Public-Private Partnership framework in February 2025. “This is beyond a Cross River dream. It is a Nigerian project. It is a poverty breaker,” he said. President Kashim Shettima at the ceremony in Bakassi on Friday Tinubu stressed that the Bakassi port would complement, rather than compete with, Lagos, which handles more than 80 per cent of Nigeria’s foreign trade. “Lagos is not our enemy. Lagos is our elder brother in trade. No country eats with one hand. No country carries all its loads on one shoulder. That shoulder will break,” he said. He argued that establishing another major maritime gateway would reduce pressure on Lagos ports, ease congestion and lower costs. “When Calabar works, Nigeria works on two legs,” the President added. He said Nigeria had not fully exploited its coastline along the Gulf of Guinea, while neighbouring countries continued to benefit from trade that could be attracted to Nigerian ports. Tinubu said the Bakassi project would help retain regional cargo, expand access to international markets and strengthen Nigeria’s competitiveness in maritime trade. He noted that about 90 per cent of cargo moves by sea, but Nigeria handles only a fraction of regional cargo trade despite its economic position in West Africa. The port, he said, would help close the gap, reduce dependence on a single maritime gateway and enable the country to capture a larger share of regional commerce. Shettima and Governor Otu at the groundbreaking event. The President also acknowledged the territorial and economic losses suffered by Cross River following the Bakassi Peninsula ruling and the loss of oil revenue. item.title: 2027: Whoever Wins Nigeria Loses, Atiku, Obi Handing Tinubu Advantage – Sule Lamido
item.description: Former Jigawa State Governor Sule Lamido has criticised opposition figures Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi for failing to unite ahead of the 2027 presidential election, saying their division gives President Bola Tinubu an advantage. Lamido, who is a chieftain of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), said a united opposition would have posed a stronger challenge to Tinubu, suggesting that Atiku could have emerged as the presidential candidate, with Obi as his running mate. He spoke on Friday during an appearance on Channels Television’s Politics Today, where he was asked whether the 2027 election could produce a similar outcome to the 2023 contest, in which Tinubu defeated Atiku and Obi. “I think the way things are, the propaganda and support warfare is too much. It’s too intense for even Nigeria to be able to really understand what’s happening,” he said. Former Jigawa governor of Jigawa State, Sule Lamido Lamido attributed the opposition’s difficulties partly to the number of serving and former governors in the All Progressives Congress (APC), as well as the failure of Atiku and Obi to work together. “Because of the number of governors, both serving and former governors of the APC, and because Atiku and Obi divided their own force, it gives Tinubu the advantage,” he said. FILE: Peter Obi (L) and Atiku Abubakar (R) The former governor argued that the two opposition leaders were effectively strengthening Tinubu’s chances by pursuing separate political ambitions. “So both Peter Obi and Atiku are simply handing Tinubu, very easily. But if they come together, it would have been a high-level canvas, you know, Atiku for president and Obi running mate, and then after four years, one takes over,” he said. ‘Whoever Wins?’ The coalition has several top politicians as members. X@ADCNig. Two years after the 2023 presidential election, Obi and Atiku left the Labour Party (LP) and PDP, respectively, to pursue a united opposition front ahead of the 2027 elections. In July 2025, opposition leaders adopted the African Democratic Congress (ADC) as a common platform to challenge President Bola Tinubu. However, internal disagreements over party leadership, structure, and presidential ambitions weakened the coalition. Kwankwaso and Obi defected to the NDC from the ADC. X/@KwankwasoRM The crisis eventually saw Obi leave the ADC alongside Rabiu Kwankwaso for the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) in May 2026, where Obi was subsequently adopted as its 2027 presidential candidate. Atiku, on the other hand, remained in the ADC and won its presidential primary. Atiku (centre) is the presidential candidate of the ADC for the 2027 general elections. Despite their separate political platforms, both opposition leaders have continued their pursuit ahead of the 2027 election. Obi has maintained that any alliance with Atiku must be based on a formal agreement between their parties, rather than a personal arrangement.
